translation:
HALIMOS (Sea Orache)

Also known as damasonion, also erymon,
also brittanike, also rabdion, also
basilike; the prophets [call it] "Hermes' foundation," like
flesh; also "Osiris's diadem";
also "crown of Pan"; also "sacred oar."
Pythagoras [calls it] anthenoros; the Egyptians
[call it] asphoin; also asontēri; also asello-
ērē; also asaraphē; the Romans call it
labukium; also ampoullakia.

The shrub is a hedge-plant, similar to buckthorn,
though not thorny, and the whole plant
is rather pale, and its leaves,
like those of the olive, are broader, however,
and softer. It grows mostly
in places near the sea, among hedges
and fences, and its leaves are
eaten. A drachma's weight of its root,
drunk with honey-water, helps against
pulled muscles, ruptures, and colic.

ALIKAKKABOS (Winter Cherry / Bladder Cherry)

Also known as dirkaion, also
"mad down," also
doryknion; the Romans [call it]
apollinaris minor, or
herba vaticana; also
ouagem; the Dacians [call it] koikol-;
the Africans [call it] kakkabum.
It has leaves similar to nightshade (strychnos),
though broader. Its
stems, as the plant
grows, become like bladders,
reddish, round, equal
in size to grape berries, and
garland-weavers use them,
weaving them into
garlands.
It has a cooling power,
so its leaves, applied as a poultice,
are good for
erysipelas and creeping sores,
mixed with barley meal.
A marvelous thing besides...

Applied crushed, it treats styes (aigilopia) and headaches,
and relieves burning fever; it is worn for parotid swellings
when crushed and applied as a poultice; and its stalk, too,
[mixed] with egg white, with silver [leaf?], and with rose oil, is good against erysipelas
and [...] against styes, when bound on.

III.

ARTEMISIA MONOCLONOS, ARTEMISIA
THE OTHER, POLYCLONOS

Some call it toxitis, others Ephesia, others parthenike,
others hypolysson, others Anactoria, others sozousa,
others leia, others leukophryx; the prophets call it "blood of man,"
the Romans ullentia, others serpullum,
others herba regia; the Gauls call it ponem, the Dacians zuzustrum.

It grows for the most part in places near the sea, resembling wormwood,
but larger and broader. One kind of it is vigorous, having broader leaves
along its stems; the other is whiter, with small, fine, strong-smelling flowers,
and it blooms in summer. Sometimes among those growing inland there is
a thinner-fruited plant with a single stalk, bearing a small flower,
pale in color, delicate, which they call artemisia.

Both kinds warm and thin the body. When boiled, they are suitable
for women's sitz-baths, to bring on menstruation, the afterbirth,
and the fetus, and for uterine obstruction and inflammation of the womb,
for breaking up stones, and for retention of urine. The herb, applied as a
plaster in quantity on the lower abdomen, brings on menstruation within a month.
The juice extracted from it, mixed with myrrh and applied as a pessary,
draws out matter from the womb; and when drunk as an enema it promotes
hair growth in the same manner.

APARINE

It has an unripe-grape-like fruit; some call it "philanthropon" (man-loving); some call it "ixos" (bird-lime). It has many long, four-angled, rough stems, with leaves set around at intervals in a circle, like those of madder. The flowers are white; the seed is hard, round, somewhat mottled, with a navel-like depression in the middle. It is also tolerated for use with milk-curdling; shepherds use this plant instead of a strainer for milk, to catch the hairs floating in it. The seed and its juices are drunk, and the leaves when pressed for juice are drunk with wine against persistent inflammations; it is also made into compresses for the ears when mixed as a poultice. The plant, mixed with fat/lard, disperses scrofulous swellings.

ASARON

It is also called wild nard. The prophets called it "limaron"; the Egyptians named it "keras" (?); the Romans [call it] "peressam"; some call it "blachaton"; the Etruscans [call it] "knoumi"; some [call it] "nardourikes"; the Gauls [call it] "baikar"—a plant [used] for garlands, also called "staphylle." It has an earthy [root] with stems that are somewhat rough between the leaves, flowers that are purple, thin, and fragrant; its roots are used like black hellebore, having the smell of cinnamon. CHAMAEDRYS · CHAMAEPITYS · CHAMELAEA ·

Also called chamairōps, also "dryïsken chros,"
also teukrion; the Romans call it tri-
gōminon; the Gauls call it kuerkia,
ereinon. It grows in rough
and rocky places; it is
a small shrub, a cubit high, having
small leaves similar in
shape and form to oak leaves, bitter; its flower is
somewhat purple and small. One should
gather it always when the fruit is forming into clusters.
It has a warming power. When drunk
with water it helps
against spasms, coughs, and an enlarged
spleen; for those with difficulty urinating
and poor digestion it brings on
menstruation and expels embryos;
when drunk together with vinegar it also helps
those with ascites when taken with wine
and applied as a poultice. Ground fine it
can also be formed into pills
as prescribed, and it cleanses
old sores when applied with honey; mixed with olive oil
and applied as a black ointment it stops
discharge from the eyes, and when smeared on
it is warming.

It also helps with hardenings and wounds, and
checks herpetic sores when applied as a poultice with honey.

Also called pitysorueis, also "oroozēn,"
also holokyron, also wild bryonia,
also "anthēnēsin," also
"aiōnian"; in Euboea it is called "sidērētis";
the prophets [call it] "blood of Athena"; the Romans
[call it] "cypress"; also "sēmeneua,"
"dakoi cholea." It is a plant
that creeps along the ground, slightly curved,
having leaves similar to houseleek
but much finer and thick,
dense along the branches, with a scent
like pine; its flowers are small
and yellowish; its root is like that of chicory.
Its leaves, drunk
with wine for seven days,
cure jaundice. It is also given
to those with liver ailments, difficulty urinating,
and kidney trouble, and is suitable
for those with colic. Use it also
for those twisted with pain.
This plant, called "Herakleia" by the

in the decoction of the herb,

when drunk, it purges the bowels; it brings on
menstruation when applied to the womb together with honey.

translation:
VII.

ASTER ATTICUS (Attic Starwort)

Also called asteriskos, also called asterion, also called boubonion, also called ophthalmos; the Romans [call it] inguinalis, the Dacians rathibida.

It has woody stalks bearing at their tips a purple flower, sometimes pale yellow, like the head of chamomile, surrounded at the top by narrow little leaves; the leaves around the stem are somewhat long and hairy. It is suitable, applied as a poultice, against inflammations of the groin while fresh; and when dried, taken up in the left hand by the sufferer and bound around the groin, it stops the pain.

AMARAKON (Marjoram) [text describes Anthemis/Chamomile]

Also called anthemis, also called leukanthemon, also called parthenion, also called chamaimelon, also called chrysokallis, also called malabathron, also called anthos pedinon; the Romans [call it] "soliseculum," also "millefolia"; the Tuscans "cautam"; the Africans "thamako"; the Gauls "vignita"; the Dacians "douodala."

Its leaves resemble those of coriander, fine and thin; its flowers are white around the edge, with a yellow center; it has a strong smell and a bitter taste.

When the dried material is drunk mixed with honey, like epithymon, it draws out phlegm and bile, and benefits those with asthma and those suffering from melancholy. This herb, apart from its flower, is also beneficial when taken as a drink for asthmatics and those suffering similarly. Its decoction serves as a sitz-bath for a womb that is irritated and inflamed. It is also applied as a poultice, together with its flowers, against erysipelas and other inflammations.

VIII.

AMBROSIA (Botrys)

Some call it botrys, some call it botrys artemisia, the Romans call it "cuprum milvaticum," others call it "apium rusticum," the Egyptians call it "merse." It is a small shrub of great beauty, with leaves like those of the wormwood, growing around the shoot of the stem; they are small, like those of rue, the branches around it bearing much seed, like small clusters, which never wither. It is sown like poppy seeds; its root sends out many shoots in Cappadocia, and it is used for garlands. It has an astringent power over discharges, and when applied as a poultice it is repellent.

WORMWOOD (Apsinthion)

The Egyptians call it "somi," the Romans "apsinthium rusticum," or "the bitter pontic one." The best kind is that growing in Pontus and in Cappadocia, on the mountain Taurus, among the growing plants.

It has a digestive power, and it purifies those suffering within, in the stomach and bowels, driving out bile. It is also diuretic, and when drunk beforehand with a bit of Celtic nard it helps against loss of appetite, and it cures jaundice when drunk continually each day in a cup along with three cyathi [measures], taken also for relief, with honey, against drowning victims and those being strangled, when drunk with wine; and against indigestion and poisoning.

It also helps against the sea-dragon's sting, and for those with quinsy it is applied as an ointment mixed together; for dimness of sight and the surrounding region likewise, and also [for] [illegible]... its decoction is useful for excessive [inflammation], and with honey-wine it serves as a poultice for painful eyes [illegible]... as a remedy it is applied to the hypochondria and the [illegible]... stomach; for those suffering chronic illness it relieves them when combined [illegible]... myrtle oil suits the stomach, and rose oil [illegible]... for dropsical patients mixed likewise with soda and nitre and [illegible].

translation: There is also prepared a wine called "wormwood wine," especially in Italy, around the Propontis and Thrace; and it is used for the purposes already mentioned. People drink it regularly when free of fever, and otherwise always drink a toast of it, believing that in summer it promotes health. It is also thought that when woven in among garments stored in chests, it keeps them from being eaten by moths; and when rubbed on the body together with oil, it prevents gnats from settling on the skin.

IX.

Abrotanon (southernwood), no. 23                           Okimos (basil)
                                                              Latin: Linus

ABROTONON                                                    OKIMOS

Some call it abrotonon, some wormwood (apsinthion), some Herakleion,
some ankona, some apogalon, some merikon,
some choloptoion, some thelyphthorion, some
apsinthiomenon, some prokampylon; the prophets [call it]
nevraphoinikos; some kynanchitis; the Romans
[call it] absinthium ponticum; some call it
lythamnos, a tree-like plant with whitish
small leaves, like wormwood from Seriphos, growing around rocky places,
all of it bears a corymb-like tip,
golden in color, appearing in summer, fragrant,
somewhat bitter in taste. The
Sicilian kind seems to be of this sort, but there is another, coarser
one called "matodes," with thin stems, like
wormwood, growing abundantly in Cappadocia and Galatia,
in the part toward Asia, and also at Hierapolis in
Syria.

The seed of these plants, taken with water
and crushed raw and drunk, helps against orthopnea (difficulty breathing),
ruptures, convulsions, sciatica, difficulty urinating, suppression of
menstruation, and serves as an antidote to deadly
poisons when mixed with wine and applied as a liniment.
Burnt together with olive oil, it drives away pests;
when fumigated and drunk with wine it benefits those in pain;
it specifically treats spider and scorpion bites; it also helps
inflammations of the follicles when boiled with henna oil
and applied as a poultice with bread, it dissolves
and tumors; mixed with honey it is beneficial;
it is also mixed into the preparation of laurel oil.

X.

ARGEMONE

Some call it anthemis, others oinone, others homonoia, others anthos pelinon; the Romans [call it] livornia, others concordialis, others pergalia; the Gauls [call it] korna.
Argemone resembles the wild poppy and the anemone; it differs in having its head somewhat flattened above... [and in] not being purple like the poppy, and it has a round root. Then it exudes a saffron-colored [juice], which [when drawn off like] opium produces... a cleansing effect on argemon (a disease of the eye) and on cataract (nephelion), and it soothes inflammations when the leaves are applied as a poultice.

ANOTHER ARGEMONE

Some call it artemone, others arsela, others sarkokolla; the Romans [call it] argemonia.
This one too resembles the wild poppy in its leaves. It has the property, when fresh and ground fine and applied, of healing inflammations of the eyes and of treating cuts. It is also good for dysentery sufferers when drunk with water; it is adhesive for wounds and inflammations of the sinews. Likewise, applied externally, it is effective for spasms and pains. It is also suitable for those bitten by venomous creatures when taken with wine.

SMALL JUNIPER                                    LARGE JUNIPER

Some call it arkeuthis, others mnesitheos,         Some call it wild cypress,

There is a small kind and a large kind. Both are resinous and have diuretic properties; when burned as incense they drive away wild beasts. Their fruit is fragrant, sweet, warming, and diuretic, and is taken for chronic coughs and flatulence. The juniper is called "black"; its leaves are pungent, so that when applied as a poultice or drunk—both the leaves themselves and their juice mixed with wine—they are effective against snakebite. The bark, when burned and applied with water, clears up skin eruptions (leprosy); and the sawdust of the wood, when drunk, is purgative/expels [worms].

Anemone, the Purple (Phoenician) One                Anemone,
                                                     the Wild Black One

Some call it "anemonion," some "mekonion,"
or "mekonis," others "tragokeros" (goat-horn), others
"ge spareine," others "barbyde." Osthanes calls it "beryllios."
Ornios calls it "keranios." Pythagoras calls it "daktylis."              Some call it
The prophets call it "wild knekos." The Romans call it "orbitounikam."   wild anemone,
The Africans call it "chouphphoist."                                    others call it
                                                                         "black" anemone.
There is a wild kind and a cultivated kind, and of the cultivated kind one bears
purple flowers, another whitish, milk-colored ones, another has purple
flowers and leaves like coriander, more finely divided, lying close
to the ground, with thin, downy, hollow stems; small flowers
like those of the poppy, and in the middle, black or dark-blue heads.
The root is about the size of an olive, or larger, like a bulb,
covered with a thin skin. Both kinds have an acrid property, so
that the juice of their root, poured into the nostrils, purges
the head. The root, when chewed, draws out phlegm. It is also
good taken in sweet wine, and when applied as a plaster it heals
inflammations of the eyes and scars on the eyes, and clears away
dimness of sight. It also cleanses sores beneath the eyelids. The
leaves and stems, boiled together and so prepared, likewise when
taken as the rest are, bring on menstruation when placed as a
pessary for several months; and when applied as a plaster, they
draw out [disperse] boils.

Some call it polytrichon, some trichomanes;        Some call it trichomanes,

They grow in shady places and around moist ground. Their stalks are black,
smooth, and glossy; the leaves resemble fern, small and smooth. The underside of
the leaves has lentil-like marks arranged opposite one another along the stalks. They
bear neither stem nor flower; the roots are of no use.

A decoction of the herb can help those suffocating with asthma,
jaundice, and difficulty in urinating. It also breaks up stones, settles the bowels,
and helps those bitten by dogs; it clears phlegm from the stomach, and
brings on the menses — it brings on the menses — and dissolves bile, and helps
with the coughing up of blood. It is also applied as a poultice against the bites of
venomous creatures, and against alopecia (hair loss); it thickens scrofulous swellings,
disperses abscesses, scurf,
and watery discharges, mixed with lye, with ladanum, myrtle oil, and wine,
used generally as a cleansing wash. It also makes roosters and
quails more pugnacious when mixed into their feed.

Some call it areitis, some aigeitis,     Some call it korchoron, some alikakkabon,
some saureitis; prophets call it         some ailouron, some ailourophthalmon,
"blood-of-the-eye"; some call it         some zeimiauros; prophets call it "night-waker",
chelidonion; the Romans call it makia,   some call it pelageitis, oxythanes, chelidonion,
some antoura, some toura, some           the Egyptians call it meikie, the Romans
touradoupago; the Tuscans call it        mekiatoura, some antoura;
masytepos, the Gauls sappana,            the Tuscans call it "tantoum," the Africans
the Dacians kerker, the Africans atirsisoei  [call it something illegible]

Of pimpernel there are two kinds, differing from one another in the color of the flower. The one having a blue flower is called the female, while the one with the red flower is called the male. Both are shrubby plants, spreading over the ground, having leaves set upon four-sided stems; the leaves are small and somewhat rounded like those of a small grape-cluster, and the fruit is round. Both kinds are soothing and anti-inflammatory; they help draw out splinters and are useful as a nasal rinse. They relieve toothache if poured into the nostril opposite the aching tooth. They clear away pain when mixed with Attic honey, and help with dimness of sight. Drunk with wine, they help those bitten by vipers, as well as people suffering from dropsy and liver ailments. Some say that the one with the blue flower helps reduce swelling of the spleen, while the red-flowered one, when applied as a poultice, causes irritation.

ANCHOUSA · ANCHOUSA ETERA (Another Anchousa)

XVI.

Some call it katarchousa, others Libyke, others
archibellion, others alkeibiadion, others onoche,
others porphyris, others medousa, others salyx,
others noneas; the Africans call it bouïnesath.
Its leaves resemble those of lettuce,
rough, dark, numerous, spreading out in all directions
from the root, pressed close to the ground, forming a clump.
It has a root about the thickness of a finger, of a
blood-red color, which grows in the ground and
stains the hands when touched. Its flowers are purple.
It grows in rich soil. The root is
astringent and, when mixed with wax and oil,
is applied to heal wounds that occur spontaneously; for
erysipelas it is applied mixed with barley meal, like a plaster, and cures it; it also treats
skin eruptions and leprosy, when ground together with vinegar and applied.
Applied as a pessary, it also brings about abortion.
Its decoction is given
to those suffering from jaundice, kidney disease, and spleen disease,
and to fever patients, mixed with honey-water. Its leaves,
drunk with wine, check diarrhea.
Perfumers also use the root for
fixing the scent of perfumes.

Right margin: "Ankusa etera; anx(ousa) ysa etera"

Others call it alkeibiadion, and the "lip-herb" (cheiles) as some name it.
This plant differs from
the first kind in having
smaller leaves, which are likewise
rough; its stems are thin,
bearing a purple-colored
flower tinged with red. Its root is
red, fairly long, tapering to
a point, having
a blood-like color.
These plants grow in sandy places.
Their power, and that of
the leaves, helps those bitten
by wild animals, especially those bitten
by vipers: eaten,
or drunk, or simply touched
to the wound, and even when chewed
and placed in the mouth
of the creature—if one then spits it out,
it will kill the creature itself.

translation:
XVII.

ALYSSON

Some call it aspidion, others apophyllon
trachy, others akkysiton, others
call it alyseton.
It has round leaves similar to [cress];
the fruit is like little shields, double,
in which is the seed. Taken, it checks
fevers accompanied by thirst, and
held in the hand or smelled, it does
the same thing. With honey it clears
away freckles and skin blemishes. It is
also thought to cure the madness
caused by a dog's bite, when pounded
and bound as a poultice on the bite,
and when hung up in a house it is
said to be a protection against the evil
eye for both people and animals.
Tied on with a piece of purple cloth,
it drives away disease in livestock.

...growing on the Taurus mountains in Cappadocia,
after the "trumpet-plants" [salpingia];
the local people call it sandonikon, named
after its resemblance to wormwood (apsinthion);
since it has a somewhat bitter seed, it can
do these same things.

SEA WORMWOOD (ABSINTHIUM THALASSIUM)

Some call it sandonikon;
others call it seriphon; the Romans call it
sandonicum. Some also call the seriphon
"sea wormwood" (apsinthion thalassion), which grows
most abundantly on the Taurus mountain range
in Cappadocia, and in the regions around
Egypt, where it is used by the priests
in place of the palm branch. It is a plant
with fine, thin twigs, resembling small
southernwood, full of seed,
somewhat bitter, bad for the stomach,
heavy-smelling, astringent, with a
warming quality throughout. When taken
by itself or with rice, or
taken with honey, it kills round
worms, expelling them gently.
It can also, boiled together with
lentils, do the same things;
it is especially recommended for this use.
There is also a third kind.

ASCLEPIAS

Some call it kission, others call it kissophyllon ("ivy-leaf"). It sends up long stalks... its leaves are like ivy. It has long, fragrant roots, a heavy-smelling flower, and seed like small dishes (lekiskoi). It grows in the mountains.

Its roots are helpful when drunk in wine for those with griping pains and for those bitten by venomous creatures. The leaves are good for malignant conditions of the womb and of the breasts.

AMMONIACUM

Some call it agasyllon, the plant from which ammoniacum comes; others call it ammoniac incense; others call it krithos; the Romans call it "helioustros," that is, "ammoniaca." This is the gum of a kind of giant fennel (narthex) that grows in the region of Cyrene in Libya.

One should choose the kind that is well-colored, free of wood, frankincense-like, clean in its lumps, and dense, having no impurity, with a root-like smell, and bitter to the taste. Such a lump is called "eryma"; the oily, earthy mass that is mixed in Libya with the ammoniac is the juice of a kind of green giant fennel.

It has a softening, drawing, and dissolving power against hardened swellings; it also purges the bowels somewhat, and it relieves pains of the joints and of sciatica. It helps also those with dropsy, with orthopnea (difficulty breathing while lying flat), and with epilepsy, when licked up with vinegar for those with fluid retention, taken with honey, or sipped with barley-water (ptisane).

It brings on bloody urine; it cleanses white spots (leukomata) on the eyes and roughness of the eyelids; it dissolves these when mixed with vinegar and applied. It relieves enlarged spleens and excessive hardenings, as well as calluses around the joints, when applied as a poultice with honey — it may even cause [something, illegible] to come out. It is also good for bruises and sciatica when rubbed on, mixed with soda (nitron) and vinegar, and with oil of henna (kyprinon elaion).

XIX.

ANDROSAKES

Some call it pikras, some leuke,
some call it the sea-plant (thalassia).
It occurs in three kinds, in
places by the sea.
One is white, with thin straw-like stems,
bitter leaves, and a small pouch
on top of its head containing
seed.
It has a drying power; taken in
wine to the amount of two drachms,
it draws out much urine in cases
of dropsy. The decoction of the
plant, and the fruit, when drunk,
does the same. It is also applied
as a poultice, beneficially, for
those suffering from gout.

ANTHYLLIS

Some call it anthyllon, some anthemis,
some leukanthemon, some choranthemis,
some call it pedinon; the Romans
call it solastrum. There are two
kinds: one has leaves similar
to those of sage, and a stem a
span in height; likewise its leaves
are soft. Its root is thin and long.
It grows in sunny sandy places.
When tasted it is somewhat salty.
The other kind resembles chamaepitys
(ground-pine) both in its leaves and its
stems, but is more hairy and rough.
Its flower is purplish, more hairy,
with a strong heavy smell; its root
is like that of a kiborion (seed-pod).
It is able to help those with
difficult urination and kidney
troubles, when drunk in quantity.
It softens inflammations; applied,
ground fine with rose oil and milk,
to the womb area, it also heals
wounds. The one that resembles
chamaepitys, among other uses,
also cures epileptics.

ANDRAPHAXYS (Orache)

It is also called andraphax, also chry-
solachanon by the Greeks, "atriplicem"
by the Romans, by the Egyptians
ochei — a vegetable
commonly known, of two kinds,
one wild, the other cultivated
and eaten as a vegetable.
Boiled, it is
softening to the bowels; applied as a
poultice, whether raw or
boiled, it relieves inflammations and swellings.
Its seed, drunk
with honeyed water,
cures jaundice.

AKTE (Elder)

It is also called "the bear's tree," also the
cultivated kind; the Romans call it
"sambucum," the Gauls
"skobeem," the Dacians "seva," the [Scythians?] "diska."
It is indeed a tree with branches
that are reed-like and round,
somewhat mottled and quite long; its
leaves, five or six to
each joint along the stalks, resemble
royal walnut leaves,
but are heavy-smelling and more bitter.
At the tips of the branches are twigs
rounded, bearing white flowers
and fruit resembling that of the terebinth,
black with a purplish tinge, [from which]
one presses out a great deal of a wine-like juice.
Its leaves, steeped thoroughly
in water and applied,
relieve inflammations.

translation:
XXI.

Darnel (its Latin name is "lolium"). The darnel that grows among the wheat in the same field has an astringent power for sores and gangrenous ulcers. Applied as a plaster with radish and salt it heals wild lichen (skin eruptions); with sulphur and pitch it treats them. Boiled in wine with pigeon dung and linseed it cures scrofulous swellings; it breaks open undigested abscesses and relieves sciatica. Boiled with honey-water and applied as a plaster with barley meal, together with myrrh, frankincense, or saffron, and fumigated with it, it helps conception.

Arktion, or Prosopis (Burdock). It is also called prosopion, potamogeiton, Persian sinepi, panakia, krenion, olasti, and apareine; the Romans call it "personacia," others call it "lappa." Its leaves resemble those of the gourd, but are larger, harder, and darker, and hairy; the stem is somewhat whitish. The root is large, black on the surface and white within. Taken in a dose of one drachm with pine nuts, it helps those spitting blood and those suffering from burning fevers, as well as pains arising from strains around the loins, when crushed and applied as a plaster. The leaves too are beneficially applied as a plaster to old sores.

translation:
XXV.

ACONITE, ANOTHER KIND
Which some call wolfsbane.
It grows again in Italy
in the mountains called the Vestine mountains,
differing from the previous kind.
It has leaves like the plane tree,
but more deeply divided and
much larger and darker.
Its stem is like that of fern,
tall, about a cubit high or even
taller. Its fruit is in pods
of considerable length, bent downward. Its roots
are intertwined like those
of crayfish, black. These are used
for hunting wolves,
being placed inside raw meat;
for the wolves, having eaten it, die.

APOCYNUM (DOGBANE)
Some call it kynanchon, others pardaliagches,
others kynomoron, others kynoktonon,
others ophaleos, others
kynanchen, others oligoros,
others heptomanios, others onestis,
others ophioskordon, others kynarike,
others elaphoskordon; the prophets [call it]
paralysis; the Romans, wild cabbage (brassica rustica);
others, kakina.
It is a shrub having long
branches, pliant and hard to break,
with leaves like ivy but softer,
dark at the tip, with a nutlike smell beneath,
full of a milky-colored sap. Its fruit
is like a bean pod, somewhat more than
a finger's length, pouch-like,
containing hard black little seeds.
Its leaves and branches,
when thrown to or placed before
wolves, foxes, and leopards,
immediately paralyze their hips.

translation:
XXVI.

ARCTION (Burdock)

Some call it arctokouron,
and its leaves are like those of mullein (phlommos),
but hairier
and rounder; the root
is entirely white and sweet,
the stem long and soft,
the fruit small, resembling
cumin.

This plant's root and fruit,
boiled together in wine
and held in the mouth,
soothes toothache; and when poured on burns
and chilblains,
it treats them. It also helps
against sciatica and difficulty in urination... [illegible]

WILD VINE (Ampelos Agria)

It sends up shoots like the tips
of a wine-bearing vine,
woody, with rough bark
that peels. Its leaves are similar to garden nightshade,
but broader and
smaller. The flower is hair-like
and foul-smelling.
The fruit resembles small clusters of grapes,
turning red when ripe.
The vine's branch is round,
like berries. This plant's root,
boiled in water and drunk,
or mixed with wine and seawater,
purges the bowels.
It is given to those suffering from dropsy. Its clusters
clear away freckles and all
blemishes. The young shoots,
freshly grown,
are also prepared for eating.

Marginal notes: "lychnion"; "strychnos agria" (wild nightshade); "vitis agria" (Latin: wild vine).

translation:
Folio mark: 1.χ.νη

Plate XXVII.

BOUNION

Some call it aton, some call it akteinē, some call it anemosphoron; the prophets [call it] parodakry; the Egyptians [call it] erxōn; the Romans [call it] skōparēgia; the Africans [call it] gizar; some call it thempsō.

It sends up a four-cornered stalk, and on it branches covered with small leaves and flowers, much-branched and of good height, finger-like. The leaves near the root are like celery but much finer, toward that of the [plant called] "triobolos." The flower is like the anemone's; the seed is like henbane, but smaller. It is diuretic and warming, and brings on the second [menstrual flow]. It is good for the spleen, kidneys, and bladder. It is used both fresh and dried, pressed into juice together with its roots and leaves, mixed with honey-wine.

[marginal gloss: binion / gropareggia (?)]

BOUPHTHALMON

Some call it balsamenē; the prophets call it laouron; some call it gonospermou; some call it gonosaphthitos; some call it mēnistheos; the Romans [call it] kappakorōnia; the Africans [call it] narou.

It sends up delicate stalks, and leaves like fennel. The flowers are yellow, larger than those of chamomile, resembling eyes — hence its name ("ox-eye"). It grows in plains and around cities. Its flowers, crushed together with wax ointment, heal swellings and hard lumps. They also say that if applied in the bath afterward, it relieves the pallor of long fasting and, for a time, improves the complexion of those with jaundice.

[marginal gloss: bifinalmon / buphthalmon / "ox-eye" (oculus bovis)]

[chapter mark] XXVIII. [chapter mark] [page number 28]

Bouglosson (ox-tongue) — "lingua bovina" [Latin: cow's tongue] — Bolbos (bulb)
[marginal: buglossa] [marginal: bolbos]

The prophets call it gonosailourou; Ostanes calls it sannouchi; the Egyptians call it antoeurin besor; the Romans call it lingua bovum (ox-tongue); others call it likanei; the Africans call it lasounaaph; the Dacians call it boudathla. Its leaf resembles bark, rough and dark, somewhat smaller, similar to an ox's tongue — which, when dropped into wine, is said to produce cheerfulness.

The bulb (bolbos) is edible, good for the stomach, reddish, and bitter when freshly dug from the ground; it has a squill-like quality and is more stomach-soothing. All varieties are pungent and heating, stimulating sexual desire; they irritate the... and, when applied with vinegar, are nourishing and medicinal, promoting fertility and inducing flatulence. When made into a poultice, they help against bruises, splinters, and thorn-wounds, as well as pains, gangrene, and... when combined with honey, they also draw things out; and when applied to dropsical swellings and dog bites, similarly mixed with honey, they help. Mixed with pepper and applied as a poultice, they relieve stomach pains and chapped skin. They are also mixed with milk and administered with aged wine for... and for soothing the gums and loosening the bowels, either alone or with a little honey, and for freckles when mixed with honey.

translation:
XXIX.

BETONICA · · BECHION (Coltsfoot)

The Romans call it Vettonica. It has leaves similar to wild dock, but larger and hairier, astringent in taste. It sends up a stem that is not large, with a thin and short root. Its leaves are pressed for juice while fresh, and this is gathered up. It has an astringent property, particularly good for ulcers of the mouth and tonsils, and it is useful for leukomas (white spots on the eye) and wherever astringency is needed.

Bechion — some call it rhechion, others petrine, others peganon, others pithion, others pagonagon, others chamaileuke, others procheton, others arkophyllon, others chamaigeiron; the Egyptians call it saar thra; the Romans call it tussilago, others pharphara; others poustoulago; the Bessi call it asa.

It has leaves like ivy, but larger, growing from the root, whitish on the upper side and greenish on the underside, with many angles. It has a stem about a span long, bearing a pale yellow flower in spring, which it quickly sheds — and at that time the stem too — so that some have supposed the plant to be stemless and flowerless. The root is thin. It grows around meadows and in moist places.

Its leaves, when dried and applied as a poultice, are helpful against erysipelas and all kinds of inflammation. When the root is burned and its smoke inhaled through the open mouth, it cures those troubled by a dry cough; it also dissolves abscesses in the chest. And the root, fumigated [and mixed] in dead wine lees, is drunk boiled in hydromel (honey-water).

XXX.

BRATHY. Savin. [number 77]
(marginal: "brathy")

Some call it barytonon; the Romans call it "herba savina"; some call it "ligon"; it is also called "komenkomi"; it resembles the tamarisk, or rather the cypress, being curly-haired (bushy) in its branches. It is more astringent in its leaves and more prickly, sharp and fiery; it breaks up swellings when applied with wine; drunk, it brings on menstruation and promotes urination, and draws blood.

WHITE BRYONY
[number 77 i]     (marginal: "bryonia leky, i.e. alba")

Some call it "madon," some "white vine," some "psilothron," some "melothron," some "ophiostaphyle," some "archezostis," some "kedrosis"; the Egyptians call it "challamos"; the Romans call it "notia"; some call it "herba cararia"; some call it "cucurbita erratica"; the Dacians call it "kinoudoila"; the Syrians "chachabiaria." It is a thorny shrub, and both its leaves and tendrils [are like those of] the cultivated vine, but rougher; and the whole plant twines about its neighbors, clinging with its tendrils. It bears a cluster-like fruit, with which hides are tanned. The young shoots at their first sprouting, when boiled and eaten, promote urination and loosen the bowels. It has a warming power. Its root, when drunk, is useful against [various ailments, hardened tumors, etc.], and when applied as a plaster it helps with bruises from falls; it is good for freckles and skin blemishes, and clears away spots and leprous conditions and dissolves swellings; it is suited to [various treatments], being pounded and applied to the fingers; when applied it also breaks up and disperses [afflictions], and furthermore it is mixed with other remedies. It is useful in many preparations and compounds for strengthening various parts of the body.

translation:
XXXI.

[marginal note, Latin]: bryonia nigra (also called "black bryony")
[marginal note, Latin]: ballote, also melan prasion

BLACK BRYONY: BALLOTE, OR BLACK HOREHOUND

Some call it black vine, some "cheiroma," some "boukranion"; the Romans call it [a corrupted Latin name]; others call it "batanouta," others "vitis alba"; the Africans call it "pegrina." Outwardly it resembles a cultivated vine, but more like a wild one, and its stems grow larger than any such plant, and it also takes hold of trees with its tendrils. The fruit is grape-like, green at first, but black when ripe. The root is black on the outside, but box-wood colored within. In the first sprouting, its shoots are eaten as a vegetable. They are diuretic, beneficial for the spleen, and suited for those who are paralyzed. The root has a power similar to that of the iris for the same purposes. It is also used for beasts of burden whose eyes have become clouded. The leaves, plastered on with wine, are likewise applied to sprains. Applied to burns it [relieves them]; it removes warts, and cleanses dirty ulcers when mixed with honey.

Some call it black horehound, some call it another kind of horehound, some "nophna," some "notianoskelin," some "nosprason," some "notheras," some "nochelis," some "nostelis," some "nophrys," some "gnothouris," some "gnotera" — the Romans call it "appioun," others "meditam," others "oukeraria," others "marrubium canoherinum"; the Egyptians call it "asphos," others "aiski"; the prophets call it "blood of Zion." It sends up square stems, black and hairy, several growing from a single root. The leaves are similar to those of horehound, but larger and black, somewhat round, with wider spacing along the stem, and smelling like balm — for this reason some have called it "balm-leaf" (melissophyllon). The flowers are arranged around the white stems in a ring, like a wheel. Its leaves, applied as a plaster with wine, are good for dog bites and dry them up...

...applied as warm ash, it clears away growths, and together with honey it cleanses dirty ulcers.

SEA BRYONY·                          OATS

bromas
also oats

Some call it ballaris, others iastrone, the Romans [call it] ... [by] the name [of] silla(?). It grows upon rocks and shells by the sea, resembling lettuce, slender, stemless, sufficiently astringent. It is effective against inflammations and many sores when applied as a plaster.

Some call it seiphonion, others akrospelon, the Romans [call it] avena, the Africans gymma(?). It is a plant found on the seashore, having a drying power. When boiled together with its roots in water until reduced to a third, strain the decoction, and mix in an equal amount of honey, and boil until it attains the thickness of liquid honey. Use it for ailments of the nose by soaking a cloth in it and applying it to the nostril, and it helps if done while the patient sleeps. Some also mix in dried mullein flowers and use it in this way as well. It is also made by boiling with dried roses in wine, for bad odor of the mouth.

GENTIAN

(Latin gloss: Gentiana)

It is also called "kentaurion rhiza" (centaury root), also "Gallic aloe," also "narke," also "cheironion," by the Dardanians "aloeitis," by the Romans "genneus," also "kikenda," also "kouminalis."
It is thought to have been discovered by a certain king of the Illyrians, Gentios, from whom it took its name. Its leaves near the root resemble those of the plantain (arnoglossos), like sorrel; those in the middle of the stem, and especially those near the top, are more divided and smaller. The stem is hollow, about a finger thick, and about two cubits tall, with joints set at intervals and wider gaps between them; it bears leaves and fruit that is light and chaff-like, long, resembling the long birthwort. It grows in high, shady, and well-watered places.

The root has a warming, astringent power. It helps against the bites of venomous creatures when two drachms of it, or of the flower, are drunk together with pepper, rue, and wine; of its juice, about a drachm is given for the same purpose...

GALEOPSIS (also called "dead nettle")

(Latin gloss: Galeopsis, i.e. "dead nettle")

It is also called "galaiobolon," also "galaiphos"; by the Egyptians "aithophi," by the Romans "urtica labonem" [literally "nettle that does not bite"]. It is a small, toothed shrub. In its stem and leaves it resembles the nettle, but its leaves are smoother and have quite a foul smell when rubbed. Its flowers are small and purple. It grows in hedges, along roadsides, and in waste ground.

The leaves and its juice have a dissolving power against skin eruptions, tumors, scrofulous swellings, abscesses, and growths behind the ears. It should be applied as a poultice twice a day with vinegar to make it effective; the poultice and the decoction loosen such growths beneficially. It is thus used for spreading sores, gangrene, and necrosis, applied as a poultice together with salt.

Lupine (left margin: "Lupinus")

Cultivated Lupine · Wild Lupine.

The Romans call it lupitinum (lupinum), the Egyptians brechou; it is well known.
Its flour, worked with honey, or drunk with vinegar,
drives out and expels roundworms;
and the lupines themselves, when soaked and eaten while still bitter,
do the same thing, and their decoction has the same effect
when taken with rue and pepper; for this reason it also helps
those with spleen trouble when drunk for some time against savage sores,
at the beginning of the season, against scaling, against eruptions,
and against scurf. The flour, mixed with vinegar, also brings on
menstruation and, as a pessary, draws out the embryo;
mixed with myrrh and honey and applied,
it cleanses sores, bruises,
and soothes inflammations when combined with barley meal and water.
With vinegar it also eases fistulas and boils,
and it disperses scrofulous swellings when boiled with vinegar and applied as a plaster;
it also dissolves carbuncles when boiled.
Lupines boiled in rainwater until they ferment
are used to cleanse the face, together with black chamaeleon-thistle.
Boiled with... they cure scab in sheep
when the animals are washed with the warm decoction. The root,
boiled in water and drunk, promotes urination.
Those that have been sweetened, however, weaken the stomach
and cause poor appetite.

(right column, continuing the description of the wild lupine)
The Romans call it lupinum agreste;
it is also called "wild thermos" (wild lupine),
growing in the wild,
tamer in appearance,
but smaller
in potency
than the cultivated kind.

SAVORY (THYMBRA)
Also called "mountain," also "sheep's," also "themitis," also "wild marjoram," also "ageraton." The Romans [call it] cunila rustica, also thymum, also capra rustica. The Egyptians [call it] sekemmen. It grows in rough places, similar to thyme but smaller and more slender, bearing a spike full of greenish flowers. It has the same properties as the aforementioned thyme when taken in the same way, and is also suitable for everyday [dietary] use. The cultivated savory is in every respect weaker than the wild kind, but more pleasant for eating because it lacks the wild kind's excessive sharpness.

THYME (THYMOS)
Also called "thymon," also "white thyme," also "kephalotos," also "epithymis," also "thyrsion." The Dacians [call it] mizela; [another people] call it moutouka; the Romans [call it] thymum; the Egyptians [call it] stephanoi. It is known by everyone as a small shrubby, brushwood-like plant, covered with many narrow little leaves, having small flowering heads that tend toward purple. It grows especially in rocky and poor ground.

It has a warming property. Taken with salt and vinegar, it purges phlegm from the bowels. Its decoction with honey helps those who have difficulty breathing. It expels worms, brings on menstruation, expels the afterbirth and even the embryo [induces abortion], and is diuretic. Mixed with honey and warmed, it is good for bringing up [phlegm] from the chest. It heals fresh swellings and disperses clots of blood. It removes warts and skin growths. Applied with wine and barley meal, it relieves sciatica. It helps those with dim eyesight, and eaten as food it is beneficial; it is also useful for everyday dietary purposes as a seasoning in place of a condiment.

XXXVIII.

THYMELAIA                                   THLASPI

(label: "thymelaia")                        (marginal Latin notes: "busa pytois, also called cordi,
                                             sanguinaria"; "f."; "Naspi")

Some call it Pyrosakne. From this plant the Cnidian berry
is produced as its fruit, which is gathered. Some call it
Apolinon, others Linozostis, because the shrub is similar
in nature to flax of the broom type. It sends up thin
shoots about two cubits long like a reed; its leaves are
like those of the Chamelaea, but narrower and oilier,
somewhat sticky and gummy when chewed. Its flowers
are white, and amid them grows fruit like a small myrtle
berry, somewhat rounder, green at first and later turning
red. The outer part surrounding the fruit is hard and
black, while the inside is white; this purges bile and
phlegm downward when about twenty of the inner kernels
are crushed and given, mixed with flour or wheat-starch,
or wrapped in honeyed grape-pulp and swallowed. It is
also used to anoint and remove unwanted dry hair.

Some call it Thlaspidion, others Persian mustard, others
wild mustard, others Myiten, others Myiopteron, others
Daimophon, others the Egyptians call it Botrys, the Romans
call it Suetemsou, others Scandulacium, others Catella,
others Pedegallinaium. It is a small plant with narrow
leaves about a finger's length, lying flat on the ground,
with somewhat oily, divided tips. It sends up a thin stem
with few leaves around it. The fruit is somewhat flat at
the tip, containing a small seed resembling cress, disc-
shaped, as if it had been crushed (whence its name comes).
It has a whitish down, and grows along roadsides and in
ditches. Its seed is pungent and heating, purging bile both
upward and downward when drunk; it is also used as an
enema for sciatica. It also draws out blood and breaks up
obstructions in the stomach; it stimulates menstruation and
induces abortion.

THELYPTERIS (Female Fern) —

Some call it "nymphaea pterinon"; the Romans call it "lingua cervina" (hart's tongue). Its leaves are much like those of the (male) fern, having many outgrowths. Its roots are flat, long, somewhat yellowish within, black in parts; some are broader. When taken with honey they expel flat worms. Taken in wine, about three drachms' weight, they expel round worms. Given to women with brine, they bring on abortion, and if taken by one who is pregnant it injures the fetus. Dried and sprinkled on wounds that are hard to heal and on moist sores, they heal them; they also cure sores on the withers of beasts of burden.

THAPSIA —

Some call it "hypopion," others "pankranon," others "scammonion," others among the Romans "thelytelis" or "ferulago," others "wild ferula." The Africans call it "boidin." It is named "thapsia" because it is thought to have first been discovered on the island of Thapsos. In its whole nature it resembles the giant fennel (narthex), but its stalk is thinner than that one's, and its leaves resemble fennel, somewhat sharp. It has umbels like those of dill at the top of each branch, and the seed is broad, somewhat flat, similar to that of elecampane but smaller. The root is black on the outside, white within, large and thick-barked, and acrid; when dug up fresh it must be treated at once while the root is still moist, being treated with heat so that the cut place remains clean of foul exudate — those who dig it should anoint themselves beforehand. The root, when cut up small, is pressed for its juice by means of a press or similar device, and is dried in the sun in an earthenware vessel of suitable thickness. Those who dig it must take care not to stand where the wind blows the vapor toward them, but rather choose a spot free of wind, for it is said [to cause] blistering of the face and of any exposed parts of the body because of the vapor given off; one must therefore [guard against this] ...

(main text — a passage from Dioscorides' *De Materia Medica* on the medicinal properties of a plant's bark, root, juice, and sap:)

...of the parts, one should proceed thus. The bark of the root has a purging power, and so does the juice; and the sap, drunk with honeyed water, purges both upward and downward. Of the root itself, four obols are given together with three drachms of nettle seed; of the expressed juice, three obols; of the sap, one obol — more than this, if taken, is dangerous. It is suited for purging incorporeal afflictions, chronic pains of the sides, and conditions requiring vomiting; it should be given for such disorders mixed sweetly with food. It also has, after its purging action, a binding power — the sap and the root more than all others of equal strength. Where it is necessary to draw out matter from deep within or to bring about suppuration, this is useful. Hence the juice, when smeared on along with vinegar, and the fresh root rubbed on, thickens the skin; it removes bruises and livid marks — the root or the juice combined with frankincense or wax — but it should not remain more than two hours. If after this one applies a warm seawater fomentation, it also removes freckles when plastered on with honey, and it disperses skin discoloration and reduces swellings. The juice, applied with vinegar, is usefully smeared on; it is also applied to conditions requiring treatment around the lung, the side, the joints, or the feet. It is useful also for drawing conditions outward, for those who are not naturally warm from circumcision. It raises swellings, and it is poured on as a fomentation; it is also kneaded together with fatty substances and placed on the affected area to fill it out.

XL.

"Horse-dock"

Some call it wild dock, the Romans "rumex"-stica; there is a kind of dock, a tall plant growing in low places, in all respects similar, but larger than the smaller dock... When drunk or eaten it relaxes the bowels; applied as a plaster with honey and wax, [the roots], whether fresh or dried, differ in strength. Their roots, whether boiled or raw, when applied as a plaster, heal leprous conditions, lichen, diseased nails; and it is good to first rub the area with vinegar. They also soothe itching; a decoction of them, used as a gargle, relieves toothache when boiled in wine and used as a mouth-rinse. They also disperse scrofulous swellings and parotid tumors when boiled and applied as a plaster with wine; they also help the spleen, applied with vinegar. Some also use the root bound around the neck against scrofula. It also stops a woman's flux when applied crushed. A decoction in wine, when drunk, purges jaundice and expels stones in the bladder; it also brings on the menses, and helps those stung by scorpions.

"Horse-fennel"

Some call it "marathis," others "wild marathon"; the Egyptians call it "sampsou," the prophets "thymarnos," the Romans "feniculum agreste" (wild fennel), others call it "feniculus," others "equinus," others "mium"; the Gauls call it "sistrambo." It is a kind of wild fennel. It bears seed like cachrys (a kind of seed), and has beneath it a fragrant root, which, when drunk, helps those bitten by vipers, breaks up stones, and purges jaundice. A decoction of its leaves, when drunk, brings on milk and purges women after childbirth.

Note that fox-tail (cauda vulpina) is good for treating all fistulas, in this manner: take the juice of celandine, the juice of hound's tongue (lingua avis), and the juice of parsley and burnet (pimpinella), and let it be distilled; and the fistula wound should be kept so that day and night, with a silver cannula, or others of this kind, applied continually in dry conditions, placing it with the hands so that the pus may come out; and the wound should be kept open as is customary so that it remains suitable for the wound.

Otherwise, a spongy substance, namely the pith of elder, should be used with a sponge according to the patient's age, and a pellet should be made for a number of days — not more than thirty up to thirty-five days — and the matter should be allowed to come out, and a pure healing should occur; nourish for two [days?] and let the matter come out; with vinegar it is purified and the wound is cleansed so that the face (or wound surface) appears clear in days.

In all respects it is of great value, and an ointment of universal property should be made in parts of heat with two parts, one part of a certain substance (vulture?) and another part of vulture powder, in proportion one part to one — this is a good prescription, tested many times and effective.

I, Ybaun (?), have kept and used this remedy for twenty years, dispersed (shared) among all physicians.

XLI.

GREAT HAWKWEED · SMALL HAWKWEED · SESELI ·

Some call this "sonchos"; the Romans [call it] "lactuca herratica" (a wild lettuce); the Africans [call it] "sithilas." It sends up a reddish, rough, thorny stem, hollow underneath, with leaves split at intervals along their edge, round about like a thistle, bearing yellow flowers on somewhat elongated heads. It has an astringent power, moderately binding; for this reason it is good for a burning stomach and, applied as a plaster, for inflammations. Its juice, drunk, soothes a gnawing stomach, and the plant itself, pounded and applied as a plaster, helps those stung by scorpions.

Some also call this "sonchos"; others call it "wild endive"; the Romans [call it] "intubum agreste"; the Africans [call it] "sithiles." This one too has leaves split at intervals along the edge; it sends up tender, pale-green stems bearing yellow flowers that form a circle around. It has the same power as the plant described above.

Some call this "phasiolos" (bean) because of its resemblance to a bean: it bears a tendril curling from the top. At the top of the stem slender heads arise, full of seeds, tasting much like black cumin; its leaf is like that of anise. Its seed, drunk with honeyed water, is good for the chest, for coughing, and for those spitting blood.

XLII.

Iris
root

IRIS

The Illyrian iris is likewise called by some Thelypeleke, by others Ourania, by others Kathairon, by others Thaumastos; the Romans call it radix murrica; others call it gladiola, others hypertritis, others Consacra trix; the Egyptians call it nari. It is named from the fact that it resembles the rainbow in the sky (ouranos) by its appearance. Its leaves are like those of the gladiolus but larger, broader, and more glossy, growing opposite each other along the stalk, upon which grow flowers — some white, some yellow, some purple, and some the color of hyacinth. Its roots are jointed, firm, and fragrant; when cut, they are dried in the shade and, strung on a cord, are stored away. The Illyrian and Macedonian kinds are the best, and among these the one with a dense, somewhat stunted root, hard to break, yellowish, and very fragrant, which when crushed makes one sneeze and burns the tongue, is the better one. The second kind is white, somewhat pale in color, and pleasant to the taste when chewed. When aged, all kinds become more fragrant but lose moisture, and they retain a warming power. It is said to cleanse, and when applied as a plaster with white hellebore and sittasion it fills up ulcers with flesh and draws out what is difficult to expel; it thins thick humors, and taken as a drink with honeyed wine it has a power against head-colds (coryza).

VIOLA PURPUREA (Purple Violet)

Others call it dasypodion, others iriapeion, others wild ion (ion agrion), others kybelion; the Romans call it setianis, others murraria, others viola purpurea. Its leaf is ivy-like, but smaller and more delicate, growing up through the middle of the root. The purple kind is exceedingly fragrant, and grows in shady and rough places. Its leaves have a cooling power; when made into a plaster with barley meal, they help inflammations of the stomach, of the eyes, and of the rectum. XLIII.

Isatis
(Latin: Erica domestica)

Some call it lygion, others gnaphalion [prophetai]; the Romans call it "routa," others call it isatis; the dyers use it. It has a leaf like plantain (arnoglosson) but broader and darker, and a stalk more than a cubit tall. Its leaves, applied as a poultice, can disperse all kinds of swellings, close bleeding wounds, stop hemorrhages, and heal gangrenous sores, creeping ulcers, and erysipelas.

Wild Isatis
(Latin: Erica silvestris — "Isatis agria," no. 89)

Others call it isatis; the Romans call it "ruta minor." The wild isatis grows along roadsides. Compared to the cultivated kind, it has larger leaves, like lettuce, but thinner and much-divided stalks, rough at the tip, with leaves hanging down in great number, tongue-shaped, and a fine, fragrant seed. It has the same effects as the cultivated plant, being even more beneficial, whether drunk or applied as a plaster.

Great Centaury · Small Centaury

Some call it Narke, others Limnesion, others Maronion, others Plektronias, others Cheironias, others Limnestis; the prophets call it Blood of Heracles, the Romans Fierrei, others Unifera, others Felterrai. It has leaves like royal walnut leaves, elongated, green in color like cabbage; their rounded edges are notched like a saw. It has a stem like a deer's antler, two or three cubits long, with many side-shoots growing from the root, bearing heads similar to poppy heads but elongated; around them is a dark-blue flower; the fruit is similar to that of safflower, lodged as if in rooted thorns. The root is thick, heavy, wrapped around and full of excellent juice, which after tasting is astringent and sharp, and the juice likewise is red. It grows in certain sunny thickets and woodlands, and is abundant in Lycia, and in the Peloponnese in Elis, Arcadia, and Messene, and around Pholoe and Lycia, and in Smyrna.

The root is good for ruptures, pleurisy, difficulty breathing, cough, epilepsy, convulsions, hunger, chills, and even for those without fever; for those with fever, two drachms of the root with water help, and likewise for those who vomit blood and for the weak; it also eases pains of the womb and brings on menstruation when prepared as a pessary and applied; its juice too is helpful for this. It is also good for wounds — used fresh when pounded, or dried after being soaked and then pounded; it also draws together and binds [wounds]. When boiled, it binds meat together if one boils it with the meat. Those in Lycia extract its juice and use it instead of Lycium.

[Second column, concerning Small Centaury:]
Others call it Centaurion Tomikron [the small centaury], others Limnes, others Eleutherotes, others Amarakton; the prophets call it Blood of Heracles, the Romans call it Febris [fever-herb], others call it Fugia... ...of old [sores/wounds] and is healing when boiled, and it is also gentle to the bowels, and bilious and thick [matters are treated] by enemas; the juice from it is suitable for sciatica, stopping blood and settling [inflammation]. This same juice is also useful for eye ailments, cleansing those whose pupils are darkened; mixed with honey it also serves as an emmenagogue, bringing on menstruation and expelling the fetus when drunk. It is also suitable for those suffering ailments of the sinews.

The juice is extracted while the plant is still green and full of seed, having been soaked for five days; then it is boiled until the water is reduced by half; afterward it is strained through a cloth, the plant material having been thrown out, and it is boiled again until it reaches the proper thickness.

Some, however, cut up the plant while still green and unripe and press out the juice directly, then place it in an earthenware vessel and let it thicken in the sun, stirring constantly with a stick, and scraping off the dried portions around the edges, mixing them back in, and covering the vessel — for dew is harmful, as it prevents the juices from thickening properly. This is the method for plants whose juice is extracted from dry roots or herbs, such as gentian; but for those extracted from fresh, juicy roots or herbs by pressing, the juice thickens in the sun as already described.

In this same way thapsia, mandrake, and omphakion, and similar substances, have their juice extracted. Likewise lykion, wormwood, and hypokystis, and similar substances, are thickened by boiling in the manner already described.

KOTYLEDON: THE OTHER KOTYLEDON

Some call it skytallion, others kymbalios, others the garden of Aphrodite, others earth's navel, others stoichis, others stergethron; the Romans call it umbilicus veneris. It has leaves like [those of] a... round and hollow, with a small stalk in the middle, and a root round like an olive. The juice of this plant and of its leaves, applied with wine as an ointment or used as an enema, heals... biliary and inflammatory conditions and erysipelas; it also helps scrofulous swellings when applied as a plaster, and a burning stomach. When the leaves are eaten, they tighten [the bowels], break up stones, and promote urination; for dropsy it is given with honeyed wine. It is also used in love potions.

Some call this one kymbalion too; it is another kind of kotyledon, having broader and older leaves, like little round shields set close together, with something like an eye traced in the middle, as though marking a boundary, growing continuously, astringent to the taste, with a thin stem, bearing upon it flowers and small seeds similar to those of hypericum (St. John's wort). It makes the root grow larger, and is used for the same purposes as the other.

XLVI.

CORIANDER, ALSO CALLED KORION · SMOKE-PLANT, ALSO CALLED FUMITORY (KORYDALLIS)

The Egyptians call it ochion, and it is also known as aphroi goid, a well-known plant with a cooling power; hence, when applied as a plaster with barley-meal or bread, it cures erysipelas and shingles. Taken with honey and raisins, it heals night-blindness, and through these same means cures inflammations and carbuncles. With litharge it dissolves scrofulous swellings and tumors. Its seed, drunk with sweet wine, expels intestinal worms and promotes the generation of seed; but if taken in excess, it dangerously disturbs the mind, so one must be careful not to use too much of it. Its juice, mixed with white lead or litharge of silver and with vinegar-and-rose oil, when applied as an ointment, helps inflammations of the eyelids (or similar swellings).

It is also called korion, and also wild korion; it is also called kapnos (smoke-plant), because it makes the eyes water as if from smoke; it is also called kapneitis, also marmaritis, also kapnogorgion, also small chelidonion (celandine), also peristerion, also kantharis; also chalkokros. The Romans call it leium; it is also called fumaria. The Egyptians call it knyx; it is also called toukoi. It is a shrubby herb, with foliage resembling that of coriander or of kostos, bearing leaves that are whiter and ash-colored; its stem is mostly purplish. Its juice is sharp and pungent, and when dropped into the eyes causes tears, like smoke does, and it can check the spreading of eating sores (nomai). It is also able, when applied as a poultice mixed with other ingredients, to prevent hairs that have fallen out from the eyelids from growing back (used to remove unwanted hair). ... concerning its use in food and other matters as noted.

bruises under the eyes. For sciatica, mixed with [illegible]

BROAD-LEAVED CONYZA                        NARROW-LEAVED CONYZA

Some call it great conyza, others "dog's-urine" (kynozematis), others daphnis, others tanaxion, others phykos, others ichnos, others linosmos; the prophets call it "infant-killer" (brephoktonos); others call it anubias, others hedyosmias; the Egyptians call it keti, the Romans intubum, others call it "lesser soldier's-herb" (militaris minor), others dellaria, others febrifugia, others phragmosa, others mustaria, others kopikoledion, others pisa.

[right column:] Others call it small conyza, others panios, others libanotis; the prophets call it kronios.

There is a small kind called conyza which is more fragrant, and a larger kind, which surpasses it in the size of the shrub and has broader leaves and a heavier smell. Both resemble olive leaves in their foliage; they are downy and oily. The height of the stem in the larger kind is about a cubit, in the smaller less than a foot. The flower is loose and fluffy, pale yellow in color, small, like that of the knekos (safflower). The roots are of no use.

The shrub, together with its leaves, when burned as incense, can drive away wild beasts and repel gnats; it also kills fleas. Applied as a poultice, it is beneficial for snake-bites, for abscesses, and for wounds. Drunk with wine, the flower and the leaves promote menstruation and expel the fetus, and help against strangury, colic, and jaundice in those who partake of it. The decoction, when drunk, helps epileptics; and its decoction, when used as a sitz-bath, cleanses the womb. The juice, when applied, stops tremors. It also helps against chills when the body is anointed with it before the attack of fever. The fine-leaved kind cures headache when applied as a plaster.

CAUCALIS

Some call it caucon, or wild daucon; others call it [...]tis; Democritus calls it bryss[on]; the Romans call it pede gallinaceum; others call it pede pulli; the Egyptians call it seseli. It has a stem about a span high, or even taller, somewhat hairy, with leaves resembling celery; at the top it bears fine, hairy, fennel-like divisions, and a white, fragrant umbel-flower. This too is eaten as a vegetable, both cooked and raw. It is also diuretic when taken fresh.

CALLITRICHON

Some call it polytrichon; others trichomanes; others adianton; others xenopteron; others pteris; others pteron; others arsion; others call the plant korion. The Egyptians call it egyer, the Romans call it cincinalis; others call it tinula; others terra capillus [earth-hair]; others super tiaoum terra. [...] Its leaves resemble coriander, [...] black, strong, [...] lacking stalk. It bears neither stalk nor flower; its root is useless. But the herb itself, when drunk, can help with asthma, jaundice, and difficulty urinating; it also breaks up stones, settles the bowels, helps those bitten by dogs, and helps with discharge from the stomach. It also helps bring on menstruation and stops [bleeding], and it checks the coughing up of blood. When swallowed, it also helps against venomous bites and against alopecia (hair loss), by causing hair to grow thickly; it clears away scrofulous swellings and abscesses, [...] and mixed with myrtle [...] when fumigated and applied to the head, it makes a woman's hair grow thicker. It also makes amber-colored... and makes quails more combative when mixed into their feed. It grows in shaded, damp places, by walls, and near springs.

CYNOGLOSSUM (Hound's-tongue):          CULTIVATED HEMP:          WILD HEMP:

Some call it "plant," some "dog's-flower," some "splenion," some call it "skolymos"; the Romans call it "lingua canis," also "lingua canina." Its leaves resemble those of the broad-leaved plantain (arnoglosson), but are narrower and smaller, downy, with a stem that lies spread upon the ground. It grows in sandy places. The leaves have the power — mixed with old wine — to heal dog-bites and fox-bites and burns when applied. Drunk with wine, it also softens the bowels and relieves hunger.

Some call it "hemp," some "rope-nourisher," some "asterion"; the Romans call it "cannabis." Hemp is a plant very useful in life for the twisting of the strongest ropes. It bears leaves similar to those of the ash, ill-smelling, long hollow stems, and round fruit, which, if eaten in quantity, quenches the generative power (sexual desire). The green juice, when squeezed out and instilled into the ears, is good for earaches.

Some call it "water-plant" (hydrastine); the Romans call it "tertia." Wild hemp bears stalks similar to those of the marsh-mallow (althaea), [but] rougher, with leaves resembling those of the cultivated kind, and a root like that of the marsh-mallow. Its root has the power to disperse inflammations and swellings, and a drink made from it [helps with] ease of childbirth(?), being useful also for weaving/binding purposes.

CATANANCHE·    CATANANCHE, THE OTHER KIND

Some call it damnamete, others dionysias, others thyrsion, others demon,
others demos, others kemos, others krotion, prophets call it kemion,
the Archares call it arkopodion, the Romans call it "herba philica,"
others call it datioka, others "Jove's hair," the Dacians call it karopeom; it is of two kinds.
One of them has long leaves like crow's-foot, a thin,
rush-like root, and heads like a basket; when dried it curls
into the ground and comes to resemble the claws of a dead kite. The other
is the size of an apple tree seedling, has a small root, leaves in shape
and color like those of the olive, soft, spread flat upon the ground, and
split. It bears a small fruit with little stalks, pierced through, arranged according to the
leaves in parts — it is called "diosereksinthon" by some. Some report that both
kinds are suited for love potions, and they say that the Thessalian women use them
for this purpose.

KROTON OR KIKI (Castor Bean)                     CAPPARIS (Caper)

Some call it wild sesame, some call it Cyprian seseli, some
call it kroton; the Egyptians call it sesthamna; some
prophets call it "blood of fever"; the Romans call it ricinum;
some call it "loupa"; it is named kroton because
it resembles that animal, the tick, in the shape of its
seed. It is a plant about the size of a small fig tree,
with leaves similar to those of the plane tree but
larger and darker, and its branches are hollow like
a reed. It bears its fruit in rough clusters;
once this is stripped off, what remains resembles the
tick animal itself, from which is pressed out the so‑called
castor oil, which is not otherwise useful except
for lamps and for plasters. When purified, about
thirty seeds in number purge the bowels of phlegm
and bile and water; they also purge
the stomach, though unpleasantly and with difficulty; indeed this
purgative upsets the stomach.
When pounded and applied as a poultice it cures [something];
it also clears freckles. The leaves, when applied,
are astringent; mixed with ground barley meal they soothe
moist eyes, and they check inflammations and
hardened swellings of the breasts, erysipelas, and are
applied also to bruises and sprains.

translation: [The plant] has small reddish berries like grapes [in cluster], woody roots, large and broad. It grows in rough places and in cultivated plots. Its fruit is also preserved [salted/pickled], and when eaten, the fruit disturbs the stomach and belly; it is also thirst-inducing when eaten, [though] weaker for the stomach than the wine [variety]. The fruit of it is used sparingly; a weight of two drachms taken with wine for forty days induces urination and loosens the bowels. It helps with sciatica and paralysis. The fruit, when drunk, helps against ruptures and spasms; it brings on menstruation and clears phlegm. It stops toothache when the fruit is boiled in vinegar and used as a mouth rinse while still warm. The dry bark of the stem is suitable for the aforementioned uses and cleanses any long-standing, foul, or callused wound when applied as a poultice. It is also applied to sore gums along with unripe grapes. For aching teeth it helps; the leaves, scraped from the white [bark], and also the branches and the leaves, and the root with frankincense, dissolve indurations and scrofulous swellings. [When one] drops it into the ears with vinegar, it kills [parasites/worms].

translation:
CROCODILEA

Crocodilion is similar
to the black chamaeleon.
It grows in wooded places,
having a long, pungent root
with a smell like cress.
The root, when scraped and drunk
with water, can bring on
a great deal of blood through the nose,
and is effectively helpful
to those suffering from stones and spleen ailments.

IVY

Some call it kithra, some kissaron, some
chrysokarpos, some poietike, some
korymbethra, some nysion, some
dionysion, some eithytherion,
some persois, some kemos, some
asplenos; the Romans [call it] silva mater,
others hedera; the Gauls [call it] souibitis.
It has many varieties according to kind.
For one sort is called white, another
black, another helix. The white bears
white fruit; the black bears
black or saffron-colored fruit, which
common people also call nysion.
The helix also has fruit, and it
has small shoots and small, angular,
reddish leaves. Ivy is pungent and astringent.
Its flowers, taken up with three fingers
and drunk in wine, help those
with dysentery; it should be drunk twice a day.
Burnt and applied, it is also suitable
when mixed with wax.
The tender leaves, chewed and applied
together with bread, cure
eaten-away spleens; they also quench thirst.
The juice of the leaves and berry-clusters,
crushed with a little honey, is good
for chronic headaches when applied
as a poultice soaked in vinegar and rose oil;
mixed with oil it also heals
bruises and hemorrhages.
As for the black kind,
its berry-clusters, when drunk, cause distress of mind
and [disturb/trouble] [illegible]...

translation:
...for pain, the small round clusters [berries of ivy], warmed in rose oil, and dropped into the opposite ear, help earache; they also soothe gouty feet, and blacken the hair when the berries are applied as a plaster. The leaves, boiled with wine and applied as a poultice, are good for every kind of sore; they also heal burns, malignant sores, and freckles when applied as a plaster, as has been said [above]. 

The berries, taken as a drink, bring on the menses; and if taken in a dose of one drachm, they cause abortion. Likewise, a tender shoot of ivy, steeped in honey and inserted into the womb, brings on the menses.

The sap, when burned, [helps with] the foul odors in the nostrils and flatulence. Its gum, when applied, removes hair and kills lice when smeared on. The juice of the roots, drunk with vinegar, helps against the bites of venomous spiders (phalangia) and against sciatica.

CLYMENON (also called "volubilis")

Some call it clymenon [of the] daimon, others
periclymenon, others heliophyes
(sun-born), others hepatitis, others smilax,
others anatolikon, others dytikon,
others merginē; the Romans [call it]
volubicrum, others
usluchrumaius; the Egyptians
oziui.
It has a slender stem and leaves similar
to those of periclymenon, ivy-like,
with tendrils turning toward one another
and intertwining. The best is
that from the mountains. The whole plant
together with its root, when boiled, is pressed into juice;
it checks the belly's red flux,
being astringent and cooling. It also checks
nosebleeds. Its leaves, applied
to fresh wounds, are
effective until the wound scars over.

CACHRYS

Some call it libanotis, others kopsaimar,
others pseudokarpasos; the Romans [call it] murrarion,
others astrumrusticum; the Egyptians
[call it so]. Its fruit is called cachrys.
It has leaves thicker than fennel,
marked in a wheel-like pattern,
and a stem taller than a cubit,
with many joints from which
it bears umbels, producing a shaggy-tailed fruit,
sharp, like that of sphondylion, timely and useful,
having an effective, warming power.
It is used to soften [conditions] in pregnant women.
[Its root] is white, of good size, somewhat fragrant like
frankincense. It grows in rough
and rocky places. When applied as a plaster it
checks hemorrhoids, and is useful for wild [ulcers]
and for sciatica.
It is used in perfumes and as a remedy for many
ailments arising from the joints. The
dried roots, mixed with honey, are given for

Peucedanum (hog's fennel)

For epilepsy and for those who are "possessed" or suffer other such conditions, and for jaundice, it heals when given with pepper and wine. It is also useful as a wash, applied with oil; it is good for convulsions and ruptures. Applied as a plaster, ground together with bran-flour and vinegar, it also cleanses skin blemishes (alphos) when mixed with very sharp vinegar.

LVII.

Nettle, the cultivated kind

The other nettle

Some call it "kalyphe," others "adike"; the Romans
call it "urtica," the Egyptians "of Seleukos,"
the... [illegible]
There are two kinds of it. One is wild, broader,
and darker in its leaves, and has a fruit similar to flaxseed, but
smaller; the other has finer seed and is not as rough. The leaves
of both, applied as a poultice with salt, heal dog bites and
gangrenous sores, malignant and cancerous growths, and foul ulcers,
sprains, tumors, swollen glands, boils, and abscesses.
For conditions of the spleen it is applied with wax ointment. It is also good for
nosebleeds when the leaves, together with their juice, are applied;
and applied with myrrh it brings on the menses, and restores
prolapses of the womb. Fresh leaves applied to the genitals
stimulate desire for intercourse. Drunk with sweet wine, it opens up
the womb; taken with honey, licked up, it helps shortness of breath, pleurisy,
and pneumonia; it brings up matter from the chest; mixed with cuttlefish
and boiled together, the leaves with shellfish soothe the bowels; it relieves
flatulence and promotes urination; boiled with barley water it brings up matter from the chest; the
decoction of the leaves with a little myrrh, drunk, brings on the menses.
Its juice, gargled, reduces inflammation of the uvula.

LVIII.                                                                    58

GALLION·          GERANION                    N
                                            GERANION, ANOTHER KIND·
                                                                    Another geranion
                                                                    [Latin gloss, smaller variety]
                                                                    

Some call it gallirion, others call it gallion, because they say it curdles milk; its branches and leaves are slender and lie along the ground, and at the top it has a yellowish flower, delicate and very fragrant. This flower is applied to burns; it is mixed with rose-wax ointment and, warmed, is used as an anointing to stop hemorrhages (bleeding). It becomes like a pale unguent of this kind, serving against fatigue (a "akopon," soothing remedy) when the root is added, it relieves... It grows in marshy, grassy places.

Some call it xylophyllon, others mertryx, myrris, or cardamomon, or origanon; the prophets call it eirobrygkas; the Romans call it pulmonaria; others call it kekotria or grouina; the Africans [call it] isk'.

Its leaf resembles that of the anemone but is larger; its root is round and sweet to eat. If drunk in wine, about a drachm's weight, it relieves all pain and discomfort of the womb caused by wind. Some also call another kind of this plant "geranion," having thin, downy stalks about two spans long, with leaves like mallow, bearing at the tips of its branches fine capsules shaped like a crane's head, with beak-like points and tooth-like projections. There is, however, no medicinal use for it.

Some call it pelonitis, others tirka, or geranogeron; the Romans call it sechinastrum; the Africans [call it] isk'.
